Abstract

In this paper, we explore several threads arising from our recent joint work on arithmetic holonomy bounds, which were originally devised to prove new irrationality results based on the method of Apéry limits. We propose a new method to address effective Diophantine approximation on the projective line and the multiplicative group. This method, and all our other results in the paper, emerged from quantifying our holonomy bounds in a way that directly yields effective measures of irrationality and linear independence. Applying these to a dihedral algebraic construction, we derive good effective irrationality measures for high order roots of an algebraic number, in an approach that might be considered a multivalent continuation of the classical hypergeometric method of Thue, Siegel, and Baker. A well-known Dirichlet approximation argument of Bombieri allows one to derive from this the classical effective Diophantine theorems, hitherto only approachable by Baker’s linear forms in logarithms or by Bombieri’s equivariant Thue–Siegel method. These include the algorithmic resolution of the two-variable SS-unit equation, the Thue–Mahler equation, and the hyperelliptic and superelliptic equations, as well as the Baker–Feldman effective power sharpening of Liouville’s theorem. We also give some other applications, including irrationality measures for the classical L⁡(2,χ−3)L(2,\chi_{-3}) and the 22-adic ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5), and a new proof of the transcendence of π\pi. Due to space limitations, a full development of these ideas will be deferred to future work.

1 Effective Diophantine approximation on 𝐆m\mathbf{G}_{m}.

Denote by h:𝐆m​(𝐐¯)→[0,∞)h:\mathbf{G}_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}})\to[0,\infty) the canonical logarithmic absolute Weil height on the multiplicative group of the field of algebraic numbers, and by H:=exp⁡(h)H:=\exp(h) its exponentiated (“multiplicative”) version. We refer to Bombieri and Gubler’s book [23, § 1.5.7] for the definitions and basic properties of these notions, and in particular [23, § 1.4.3] for the normalization |⋅|v|\cdot|_{v} we will be using of the absolute value in the place v∈MKv\in M_{K} of a number field KK. These are the normalizations (see also subsection 1.1) such that, with log+⁡(t):=max⁡(0,log⁡|t|)\log^{+}(t):=\max\left(0,\log{|t|}\right) and α∈𝐐¯\alpha\in\overline{\mathbf{Q}} is arbitrary, we have h⁡(α)=∑v∈MKlog+⁡|α|vh(\alpha)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}\log^{+}{|\alpha|_{v}} independently of a choice of number field KK containing α\alpha.

A landmark theorem in Diophantine analysis takes on the following minimalistic but structurally robust form.

Theorem 1.1.

Consider the following data:

  • •

    a number field KK;

  • •

    a place vv of KK;

  • •

    a finitely generated subgroup Γ<K×\Gamma<K^{\times} of the multiplicative group 𝐆m​(K)=K×\mathbf{G}_{m}(K)=K^{\times};

  • •

    a positive number ε>0\varepsilon>0.

From these data, one can extract an effectively computable function C⁡(K,v,Γ,ε)∈𝐑C(K,v,\Gamma,\varepsilon)\in\mathbf{R}, for which the following Diophantine boundedness property takes place: For every A∈K×A\in K^{\times}, all solutions γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma of the Diophantine inequality

(1.1) |1−A​γ|v≤H​(γ)−ε|1-A\gamma|_{v}\leq H(\gamma)^{-\varepsilon}

satisfy the effective height bound

(1.2) h⁡(γ)≤C⁡(K,v,Γ,ε)​(1+h⁡(A)).h(\gamma)\leq C(K,v,\Gamma,\varepsilon)\left(1+h(A)\right).

One goal of this paper is to outline a new proof of Theorem 1.1. We begin, however, with an abridged history. Theorem 1.1 was first proved by Alan Baker [7] in the Archimedean case (enhancing his original method for lower bounds on linear forms in logarithms in many variables through ideas of Stark and Feldman), and Kunrui Yu [65] in the nonarchimedean case. The effectivity clause is the important one—it is the feature allowing for an algorithmic output of all solutions to many Diophantine equations and inequalities (in the spirit of Hilbert’s Tenth Problem). In contrast, the mere existence of some C⁡(K,v,Γ,ε)∈𝐑C(K,v,\Gamma,\varepsilon)\in\mathbf{R} follows easily from Roth’s (or indeed from Siegel’s) ineffective Diophantine exponent of an arbitrary algebraic number, as Gelfond observed based on Siegel’s argument with collecting coset representatives under a high degree isogeny [r]:𝐆m→𝐆m[r]:\mathbf{G}_{m}\to\mathbf{G}_{m}. (See, for example, [62, Theorem 1.9] for how the A=1A=1 case follows ineffectively from Roth’s theorem. The general argument for A∈K×A\in K^{\times} is similar and implicit in this reduction scheme, see also section 4 below.)

By a standard and easy argument (see [23, § 5.4.3]), the special case A=1A=1 of Theorem 1.1 (formulated as Theorem 5.4.1 in [23]) provides an effective height bound on the general SS-unit equation x+y=1x+y=1 in two variables, to be solved in the group of SS-units x,y∈𝒪K,S×x,y\in\mathcal{O}_{K,S}^{\times} in a number field KK, with S⊂MKS\subset M_{K} signifying an arbitrary finite set of places that contains all Archimedean places, namely:

(1.3) h⁡(x)+h⁡(y)≤log⁡16+2​maxv∈S​{C⁡(K,v,𝒪K,S×,12​|S|)}.h(x)+h(y)\leq\log{16}+2\max_{v\in S}\left\{C\left(K,v,\mathcal{O}_{K,S}^{\times},\frac{1}{2|S|}\right)\right\}.

In turn, by the classical arguments of Siegel and Mahler (see [23, § 5.3] or [42, § 9.6]), an effective height bound Eq. 1.3 leads in theory to an algorithmic resolution of the general Thue–Mahler F⁡(x,y)∈𝒪K,S×F(x,y)\in\mathcal{O}_{K,S}^{\times} and superelliptic ym=f⁡(x)y^{m}=f(x) equations in SS-integers x,y∈𝒪K,Sx,y\in\mathcal{O}_{K,S}, and more broadly to compute the set of integral points on various other (although far from all) affine algebraic curves. Here, F⁡(x,y)∈K⁡[x,y]F(x,y)\in K[x,y] is an arbitrary homogeneous form and f⁡(x)∈K⁡[x]f(x)\in K[x] is an arbitrary polynomial. Furthermore, the linear dependence in Equation 1.2 on the parameter h⁡(A)h(A), which in the Archimedean case is formulated and proved as Baker’s Theorem 1.10 in [30, §§ 1, 4, 11, E], also allows one (via the Thue equation, see [30, §§ 4.3, 4.4]) to derive a form of the Baker–Feldman theorem [43] on the effective improvement μeff​(α)≤deg⁡α−ϵ⁡(𝐐⁡(α))\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}(\alpha)\leq\deg{\alpha}-\epsilon\left(\mathbf{Q}(\alpha)\right) of Liouville’s Diophantine exponent d=deg⁡αd=\deg{\alpha} for an arbitrary algebraic number of a degree d≥3d\geq 3.

The best (known) dependence

(1.4) C(K,v,Γ,ε)≪[K:𝐐],v,ε,t∏i=1t(1+h(ξi))C(K,v,\Gamma,\varepsilon)\ll_{[K:\mathbf{Q}],v,\varepsilon,t}\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1+h(\xi_{i}))

on the heights of a set of generators ξ1,…,ξt\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{t} of Γ\Gamma (apart from an absolute numerical coefficient involved, which however is frequently quite important in practical applications) comes from Baker’s theory of linear forms in logarithms in many variables, cf. [9] or [61, 62] in the Archimedean case, and [66, 67, 68] in the nonarchimedean case. Note that the ultimate Baker–Wüstholz dependency in the form Eq. 1.4 eliminates the special role of the coset A​ΓA\Gamma, and A=1A=1 is no longer any loss of generality in this formulation. The form Eq. 1.4 has no reason to have any finality; the most optimistic folklore conjecture closely related to a​b​cabc speculates that the product in Eq. 1.4 should get replaced by a sum. For simplicity of the exposition, we shall hence stick to the minimalistic essential form of Theorem 1.1, including the distinguished coset parameter AA in the shape of Baker’s Sharpening II [7], and we abstain from pursuing here the refinement to the form Eq. 1.4. A number of different and easier proofs [16, 29], [30, § 4.1], [62, Corollary 10.18] of  Theorem 1.1 were obtained using Bombieri’s geometry of numbers argument. The most rudimentary form of Bombieri’s idea [30, Lemma 4.2] goes back to an observation of Stark [58, page 262] which we will use ourselves in section 4. This argument only requires relatively simpler-to-prove bounds [51, 52, 31] for two logarithms, and in particular it does not require the optimal (logarithmic) dependence on the variables of the linear form (or the exponents, as one frequently says). What they do require, however, is that they come with Waldschmidt’s optimal range of uniformity in the arguments (inputs) of the logarithms. (This feature was first introduced in [61, parameter MM on page 179], see also [62, Theorem 9.1 (ii) with the modified parameter BB].)

Once the reduction to softer bounds on linear forms in two logarithms (given Waldschmidt’s uniformity feature) had been made, it opened up a second and more algebraic path to Theorem 1.1 independent from the analytic theory of linear forms in logarithms. This was carried out by Bombieri in the 1990s, grounded in a Galois equivariant form of the Thue–Siegel principle found by Bombieri, van der Poorten, and Vaaler [18, 24]. A general and completely explicit bound Eq. 1.2, which for large enough h⁡(A)h(A) is also of the Baker–Wüstholz form Eq. 1.4 (although with an inferior dependence on the implicit parameters [K:𝐐],v,ε[K:\mathbf{Q}],v,\varepsilon, and t=rank⁡(Γ)t=\mathrm{rank}\,(\Gamma)), can be found in Bombieri [17] in the Archimedean case, and Bombieri–Cohen [21] and [22] in the nonarchimedean case. Bombieri’s original work [17] was founded upon Viola’s geometric form [60] of Dyson’s nonvanishing lemma, whereupon the introduction of an extrapolation parameter thereafter in [21, 22] denoted “MM” led in [21] (worked out in detail only in the nonarchimedean case) to a logarithmically improved implicit coefficient in the final estimate of the form Eq. 1.4. Finally in [22] the appeal to Viola’s theorem was bypassed and replaced by an elementary Wronskian argument, and the final implicit coefficient in the form Eq. 1.4 (once again for h(A)≫[K:𝐐],v,ε,t1h(A)\gg_{[K:\mathbf{Q}],v,\varepsilon,t}1, and worked out there in the nonarchimedean case) was improved some further.

Ultimately, both the Baker–Waldschmidt and the Thue–Siegel (Bombieri) paths to Theorem 1.1 (the only known proofs) remain fairly complicated, and there is no easy path known to such a theorem, even in the special case A=1A=1. This is despite the central role of Theorem 1.1 in modern Diophantine analysis, and after several decades of intensive research (see [30, 8, 10, 54] for a panorama of this subject, and to [19, 20, 39] for an introduction to the paradigm’s history and some speculation about its future in the light of the famous and elusive a​b​cabc conjecture). In this paper, we give a new—and perhaps simpler—proof of Theorem 1.1 by applying our quantitative arithmetic holonomy bounds that we develop below. Explicit bounds will be given in a future paper as we continue to explore the potential of the method we outline here. Two longstanding unsolved problems in the area are to give an effective height bound on the multivariable SS-unit equation, and to effectivize Thue’s theorem for general algebraic numbers besides those of the binomial form a/br\sqrt[r]{a/b}.

1.1 Notation.

As we already said in the introduction, all our conventions and notations for heights and absolute values are the ones found in Bombieri and Gubler’s book [23]. We spell out, in particular, that |⋅|v|\cdot|_{v} is normalized so that |p|v=p−[Kv:𝐐p][K:𝐐]|p|_{v}=p^{-\frac{[K_{v}:\mathbf{Q}_{p}]}{[K:\mathbf{Q}]}} if v|pv\mid p, and |x|v=|x|∞[Kv:𝐑][K:𝐐]|x|_{v}=|x|_{\infty}^{\frac{[K_{v}:\mathbf{R}]}{[K:\mathbf{Q}]}} for v|∞v\mid\infty and |⋅|∞|\cdot|_{\infty} the Euclidean norm on Kv⊂𝐂K_{v}\subset\mathbf{C}. We let 𝐃v​(R)\mathbf{D}_{v}(R) and 𝐃¯v​(R)\overline{\mathbf{D}}_{v}(R) denote the open and closed unit discs of radius RR in 𝐂v\mathbf{C}_{v}, and 𝐓v(R)=∂𝐃¯v(R):={|x|v=R}\mathbf{T}_{v}(R)=\partial\overline{\mathbf{D}}_{v}(R):=\{|x|_{v}=R\}; we sometimes omit the subscript when v=∞v=\infty, and we also abridge 𝐃v:=𝐃v​(1)\mathbf{D}_{v}:=\mathbf{D}_{v}(1), 𝐃¯v:=𝐃¯v​(1)\overline{\mathbf{D}}_{v}:=\overline{\mathbf{D}}_{v}(1), 𝐓v:=𝐓v​(1)\mathbf{T}_{v}:=\mathbf{T}_{v}(1). More generally, we follow the notation of [34]. We will use c0c_{0}, c1,…c_{1},\ldots to denote a sequence of effective constants readily computable in a constructive function of a datum indicated within (possibly empty) brackets. Similarly, the Vinogradov symbols ≪\ll, ≍\asymp, and ≫\gg used without subscripts will imply absolute effective constants, and in general implicit constants that are effectively and straightforwardly computable in terms of the data listed in the subscript. The semantical meaning of every occurrence of those symbols is that effective implicit conditions can be written down for which the given statement holds.

2 Arithmetic holonomy bounds: a quantitative theory.

2.1 Holonomy bounds and irrationality.

Let us recall the framework in [34, § 1.2, § 2] for proving the irrationality of certain periods η\eta. We start (typically) with A⁡(x)∈𝐙​⟦x⟧A(x)\in\mathbf{Z}\llbracket x\rrbracket and B⁡(x)∈𝐐​⟦x⟧B(x)\in\mathbf{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket such that B⁡(x)−η​A​(x)B(x)-\eta A(x) has larger convergence radius than both A⁡(x)A(x) and B⁡(x)B(x) as power series in 𝐑​⟦x⟧\mathbf{R}\llbracket x\rrbracket. By analogy with [59, 15], we call η\eta an Apéry limit. We pick a holomorphic mapping φ:(𝐃¯,0)→(𝐂,0)\varphi:(\overline{\mathbf{D}},0)\rightarrow(\mathbf{C},0) such that φ∗​(B⁡(x)−η​A​(x))\varphi^{*}(B(x)-\eta A(x)) is meromorphic on 𝐃⊂𝐃¯\mathbf{D}\subset\overline{\mathbf{D}}. We then bound the largest number of 𝐐⁡(x)\mathbf{Q}(x)-linearly independent power series f1,…,fm∈𝐐⁡⟦x⟧f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in\mathbf{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket such that the denominators of their coefficients have the same shape (or better) as those of B⁡(x)B(x), and additionally that φ∗​fi\varphi^{*}f_{i} is meromorphic on 𝐃\mathbf{D} for all ii. If we assume for contradiction that η∈𝐐\eta\in\mathbf{Q}, then we can take some of these fif_{i}’s to be B⁡(x)−η​A​(x)B(x)-\eta A(x) and its derivatives, but there may exist (unconditionally) additional such functions. Our holonomy bound (see Theorem 2.1 below) provides an upper bound of mm in terms of φ\varphi and denominator types when |φ′​(0)||\varphi^{\prime}(0)| is sufficiently large comparing to the denominators. We deduce that η∉𝐐\eta\notin\mathbf{Q} precisely when we find more functions fif_{i} (including B⁡(x)−η​A​(x)B(x)-\eta A(x) and its derivatives) than the upper bound provided by the following theorem proved in [34, Theorem 2.5.1].

Theorem 2.1.

Consider two positive integers m,r∈𝐍>0m,r\in\mathbf{N}_{>0} and an m×rm\times r rectangular array of nonnegative real numbers 𝐛:=(bi,j)1≤i≤m, 1≤j≤r,\mathbf{b}:=\big(b_{i,j}\big)_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq m,\,1\leq j\leq r\end{subarray}}, all of whose columns have the form 0=b1,j=⋯=buj,j<buj+1,j=⋯=bm,j=:bj0=b_{1,j}=\cdots=b_{u_{j},j}<b_{u_{j}+1,j}=\cdots=b_{m,j}=:b_{j}, ∀j=1,…,r,\forall j=1,\ldots,r, for some uj∈{0,1,…,m}u_{j}\in\{0,1,\ldots,m\} depending on the column. Let σi:=bi,1+…+bi,r,i=1,…,m\sigma_{i}:=b_{i,1}+\ldots+b_{i,r},\,i=1,\ldots,m be the ii-th row sum, and define τ⁡(𝐛):=1m2​∑i=1m(2​i−1)​σi=σm−1m2​∑j=1ruj2​bj∈[0,σm]\displaystyle\tau(\mathbf{b}):=\frac{1}{m^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}(2i-1)\sigma_{i}=\sigma_{m}-\frac{1}{m^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{r}u_{j}^{2}b_{j}\in[0,\sigma_{m}].

Remark 2.2.

In [34, §§ 6–8], we allow more general denominators of fif_{i}, and we have various improvements and alternative bounds. For the rest of this section, we will discuss upper bounds on the irrationality measure of η\eta and use the bound Eq. 2.2 as a showcase. We hope it will be clear to the reader how the proof idea of Theorem 2.6 can be used to refine all our qualitative holonomy bounds in [34, §§ 6–8] to include an irrationality measure. By the same token, simpler proofs of the bounds needed for the application to Theorem 1.1 can be more directly obtained with the Perelli–Zannier dynamic box principle technique that we explain in [34, Appendix B].

2.2 Irrationality measures.

We recall the definition of irrationality measure.

Definition 2.3.

Let vv be a place of 𝐐\mathbf{Q}. The irrationality exponent/measure of η∈𝐐v∖𝐐\eta\in\mathbf{Q}_{v}\smallsetminus\mathbf{Q}, denoted by μ⁡(η)\mu(\eta), is the supremum of the set of numbers κ\kappa such that 0<|η−pq|v<1qκ\displaystyle 0<\left|\eta-\frac{p}{q}\right|_{v}<\frac{1}{q^{\kappa}} is satisfied by infinitely many (p,q)∈𝐙×𝐙>0(p,q)\in\mathbf{Z}\times\mathbf{Z}_{>0}.

In other words, for κ>μ⁡(η)\kappa>\mu(\eta), the above inequality only has finitely many solutions (p,q)(p,q) as above; thus there exists a constant C=C⁡(η,κ)∈𝐑>0C=C(\eta,\kappa)\in\mathbf{R}_{>0} such that for all (p,q)∈𝐙×𝐙>0(p,q)\in\mathbf{Z}\times\mathbf{Z}_{>0}, we have |η−pq|v>Cqκ\displaystyle\left|\eta-\frac{p}{q}\right|_{v}>\frac{C}{q^{\kappa}}. When η\eta is algebraic of degree d≥2d\geq 2, Liouville’s theorem [54, ch. 1 § 1.6] gives κ=d\kappa=d with an effective constant CC, and in this case there is a distinction to be made between Definition 2.3 (which, by Roth’s theorem, reads μ⁡(η)=2\mu(\eta)=2 whenever 2≤[𝐐(η):𝐐]<∞2\leq[\mathbf{Q}(\eta):\mathbf{Q}]<\infty), and exponents κ\kappa for which an explicit C⁡(η,κ)C(\eta,\kappa) can be provided. The infimum of the latter κ\kappa, though this not a mathematical definition, is commonly denoted μeff​(η)\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}(\eta), and it is the notion featured in all our theorems in this paper (see Remark 2.7). We denote by μeff,K,v​(η)\mu_{\mathrm{eff},K,v}(\eta) the straightforward generalization over a number field KK and place v∈MKv\in M_{K} for vv-adic KK-rational approximations to an η∈Kv∖K\eta\in K_{v}\smallsetminus K.

Theorem 2.1 extends to a quantitative refinement that includes an explicit upper bound on the irrationality measure μ⁡(η)\mu(\eta) for an Apéry limit η∈𝐑∖𝐐\eta\in\mathbf{R}\smallsetminus\mathbf{Q} as considered in subsection 2.1; for concreteness we formulate our next proposition for the case of the Archimedean place of 𝐐\mathbf{Q}. Let 𝒱⁡(φ,b→,η)\mathcal{V}(\varphi,\vec{b},\eta) denote the 𝐑⁡(x)\mathbf{R}(x)-span of power series g∈𝐑​⟦x⟧g\in\mathbf{R}\llbracket x\rrbracket of form g⁡(x)=B⁡(x)−η​A​(x)g(x)=B(x)-\eta A(x) such that φ∗​g\varphi^{*}g is meromorphic on 𝐃\mathbf{D} and A⁡(x),B⁡(x)A(x),B(x) satisfy Eq. 2.3.

Proposition 2.4.

Fix φ:(𝐃¯,0)→(𝐂,0)\varphi:(\overline{\mathbf{D}},0)\to(\mathbf{C},0) and a denominator type b→\vec{b} with |φ′​(0)|>e∑j=1rbj|\varphi^{\prime}(0)|>e^{\sum_{j=1}^{r}b_{j}}. Let

m=dim𝐑⁡(x)𝒱⁡(φ,b→,η)≥dim𝐐⁡(x)𝒱⁡(φ,b→)=γ⋅m,γ∈𝐐∩(0,1].m=\dim_{\mathbf{R}(x)}\mathcal{V}(\varphi,\vec{b},\eta)\geq\dim_{\mathbf{Q}(x)}\mathcal{V}(\varphi,\vec{b})=\gamma\cdot m,\quad\gamma\in\mathbf{Q}\cap(0,1].

If we set μ⁡(η)→∞\mu(\eta)\rightarrow\infty in Eq. 2.4, we recover Eq. 2.2. In particular, every qualitative irrationality proof by the holonomy bounds method of Theorem 2.1 automatically refines via Eq. 2.4 to an explicit measure of irrationality. It must be said, however, that in this form of the result, the extra coefficient 22 of μ​(η)−1\mu(\eta)^{-1} in Eq. 2.4 means that, when the usual Apéry limit works, Proposition 2.4 does not recover the most basic standard bound on the irrationality measure. It remains an open problem to give an ε\varepsilon-improvement over the usual irrationality measure in every single case.

3 A dihedral method.

We begin by recalling the classical hypergeometric method [54, ch. 1, § 3], by which Thue originally proved his ineffective finiteness theorem on the integer solutions (X,Y)∈𝐙2(X,Y)\in\mathbf{Z}^{2} of the equation a​Xr−b​Yr=caX^{r}-bY^{r}=c for r≥3r\geq 3 and a,b,c∈𝐙∖{0}a,b,c\in\mathbf{Z}\smallsetminus\{0\}. The hypergeometric equation with three parameters α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma is the second-order linear ODE

x⁡(x−1)​d2​Fd​x2+((α+β+1)​x−γ)​d​Fd​x+α​β​F=0,\displaystyle x(x-1)\frac{d^{2}F}{dx^{2}}+\left((\alpha+\beta+1)x-\gamma\right)\frac{dF}{dx}+\alpha\beta F=0,

with one solution, regular at the singular point x=0x=0, being given by the power series

F⁡(x)=F12​[.α​βγ.;x]:=∑k=0∞α(α+1)⋯(α+k−1)⋅β(β+1)⋯(β+k−1)γ(γ+1)⋯(γ+k−1)​xkk!.\displaystyle F(x)={}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\alpha, \beta}{\gamma};x\right]}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)\cdots(\alpha+k-1)\cdot\beta(\beta+1)\cdots(\beta+k-1)}{\gamma(\gamma+1)\cdots(\gamma+k-1)}\,\frac{x^{k}}{k!}.

A well-known fact going back to Gauss and Jacobi [48, page 160] is that the Hermite–Padé approximants to the hypergeometric functions of the special form F12​[.α​1γ.;x]{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\alpha, 1}{\gamma};x\right]} are all explicitly given in terms of hypergeometric polynomials themselves. This applies in particular to the logarithm function log(1−x)=−x⋅F12[.1​12.;x]\log(1-x)=-x\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{1, 1}{2};x\right]} as well as the binomial functions (1−x)ν=F12​[.−ν​11.;x](1-x)^{\nu}={}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{-\nu, 1}{1};x\right]}, and we have:

(3.1) \displaystyle F12​[.−ν−n−m−m−n.;x]−(1−x)ν⋅F12​[.ν−m−n−m−n.;x]\displaystyle{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{-\nu-n,-m}{-m-n};x\right]}-(1-x)^{\nu}\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\nu-m,,-n}{-m-n};x\right]}
=(−1)m​(n+νm+n+1)(m+nm)​F12​[.−ν+m+1​n+1m+n+2.;x]​xm+n+1=(−1)m​(n+νm+n+1)(m+nm)​xm+n+1+O⁡(xm+n+2).\displaystyle=(-1)^{m}\frac{\binom{n+\nu}{m+n+1}}{\binom{m+n}{m}}{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{-\nu+ m+1 ,n+1}{m+n+2};x\right]}\,x^{m+n+1}=(-1)^{m}\frac{\binom{n+\nu}{m+n+1}}{\binom{m+n}{m}}\,x^{m+n+1}+O(x^{m+n+2}).

In a famous paper [4] in 1964 preceding his first general lower bounds on linear forms in logarithms of algebraic numbers, Baker followed the method of Thue and Siegel [57] to establish the explicit Diophantine inequality |23−p/q|>10−6​q−2.955|\sqrt[3]{2}-p/q|>10^{-6}q^{-2.955} by considering the sequence of rational approximations to 23\sqrt[3]{2} obtained from the specializations m=nm=n, ν=1/3\nu=1/3, and x:=3/128x:=3/128 in Eq. 3.1. A crucial point of the numerology is that the linear forms thus specialized in 11 and 1−3/1283=(5/8)​23\sqrt[3]{1-3/128}=(5/8)\sqrt[3]{2} have exponentially small denominators, for instance of the form (2​nn)​27​n​3⌊n/2⌋\binom{2n}{n}2^{7n}3^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}. More in line with the Apéry limits method and our holonomy bounds, the generating function of those linear forms is a GG-function in the sense of Siegel [69, § VII, page 43], obeying a certain third-order linear homogeneous ODE on the domain 𝐏1∖{0,∞,((1±1−3/128)/2)−2}\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\left\{0,\infty,\big((1\pm\sqrt{1-3/128}\,)/2\big)^{-2}\right\}, overconvergent at the first singularity ((1+1−3/128)/2)−2≈1.012((1+\sqrt{1-3/128}\,)/2)^{-2}\approx 1.012, and, as a result, holomorphic all the way up to the next singularity ((1−1−3/128)/2)−2≈28784.766((1-\sqrt{1-3/128}\,)/2)^{-2}\approx 28784.766. Chudnovsky’s improvements in [38] came from a close study of which primes dividing (2​nn)\binom{2n}{n} actually appear in the denominator, and therefore to compute the exact asymptotics of the true denominator. In more recent times, Bennett has refined the hypergeometric method, improving [11] Baker’s example to the clean bound |23−p/q|>q−2.5/4|\sqrt[3]{2}-p/q|>q^{-2.5}/4, and establishing in collaboration with de Weger the striking theorem [12, 13] that for every r≥3r\geq 3 and a,b∈𝐙a,b\in\mathbf{Z} the original Thue equation a​Xr−b​Yr=1aX^{r}-bY^{r}=1 has not more than one solution in positive integers (X,Y)∈𝐍2(X,Y)\in\mathbf{N}^{2} (in particular, by bridging the gap to the wholly complementary range of applicability of the theory of linear forms in logarithms).

3.1 Multivalence.

The behavior of the generating functions of the m=nm=n diagonal specializations of the Hermite–Padé forms Eq. 3.1—namely, that they are holonomic and overconvergent at the smallest non-zero singularity—exemplifies the mechanism of overconvergence for Apéry limits described in subsection 2.1. Following [34], we seek to continue the traditional hypergeometric method by considering the analytic continuations of these functions beyond their convergence discs. Ideally, we can find conformally large, possibly multivalent analytic mappings φ:(𝐃¯,0)→(𝐂,0)\varphi:(\overline{\mathbf{D}},0)\to(\mathbf{C},0), and then apply our holonomy bounds. To obtain better multivalence properties, it turns out to be advantageous to ignore the arithmetic denominator savings in [38], and instead take the generating function of Eq. 3.1 after first clearing through the binomial coefficient. For ν∈𝐐\nu\in\mathbf{Q}—as it turns out—we obtain an algebraic (dihedral) generating function on the domain y∈𝐏1∖{((1±1−x)/x)2,∞}y\in\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\left\{((1\pm\sqrt{1-x})\,/x)^{2},\infty\right\} (y=0y=0 is no longer a singularity!). We have the clean hypergeometric polynomial generating function identity

∑m,n=0∞F12​[.−ν−n−m−m−n.;x]​(m+nm)​ym​zn=(1−x​y)ν1−y−z+x​y​z.\sum_{m,n=0}^{\infty}{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{-\nu-n,-m}{-m-n};x\right]}\binom{m+n}{m}\,y^{m}z^{n}=\frac{(1-xy)^{\nu}}{1-y-z+xyz}.

On the m=nm=n diagonal, this gives, by a standard Cauchy integral (over a “vanishing cycle” [44, 41]):

The functions Aν​(x,y),Bν​(x,y)A_{\nu}(x,y),B_{\nu}(x,y) of Eq. 3.2 have the property that, at every finite place v∈M𝐐⁡(x,∏p|r−1p1/(p−1))finv\in M_{\mathbf{Q}(x,\prod_{p\mid r-1}p^{1/(p-1)})}^{\mathrm{fin}} when x∈𝐐¯x\in\overline{\mathbf{Q}} is algebraic, they map the closed vv-adic disc |y|v≤max⁡(1,|x|v)−1​|r​∏p|rp1/(p−1)|v|y|_{v}\leq\max(1,|x|_{v})^{-1}\,|r\prod_{p\mid r}p^{1/(p-1)}|_{v} to the closed unit disc |Y|v≤1|Y|_{v}\leq 1.

The local monodromies of Eq. 3.3 are 𝐙/2​𝐙\mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z} at the finite singularities y=((1±1−x)/x)2y=((1\pm\sqrt{1-x}\,)/x)^{2}, and 𝐙/r​𝐙\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z} at y=∞y=\infty. We take up David and Gregory Chudnovskys’ arithmetic algebraization method [37] for cases of Grothendieck’s pp-curvature conjecture (as extended by André [2, §§ 1.2–1.4] and Bost [25] when the monodromy group is a priori virtually solvable). The exponential map to a commutative algebraic group gives rise [55] to certain entire meromorphic resolutions φ\varphi (generally in several variables) of growth order ≤2\leq 2. One then exploits these resolutions to prove algebraicity (under the running hypotheses) in a manner similar to that of section 2. In our situation, we have an a priori algebraic function H=B−η​AH=B-\eta A with holonomic rank 22, but one of a high algebraicity degree ∈{r,2​r}\in\{r,2r\}, with an algebraic Apéry limit of the form η=ar\eta=\sqrt[r]{a} (if we specialize x:=1−ax:=1-a with a∈𝐐¯a\in\overline{\mathbf{Q}}); and we can take the entire map φ∈𝒪⁡(𝐂)\varphi\in\mathcal{O}(\mathbf{C}) to be holomorphic in just one single variable, and with growth order 11 (for AA and BB simultaneously), or 1/21/2 (for the overconvergent combination H:=B−η​AH:=B-\eta A). This pair of maps is universal for the general (“spherical triangle type (2,2,∞)(2,2,\infty)”) ODE on 𝐏1∖{α,β,∞}\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{\alpha,\beta,\infty\} having order 22 local monodromies around the two finite singularities α\alpha and β\beta. The latter map—crucially for our application, of growth order strictly <1<1—has never apparently been considered in this circle of problems before. In these arrangements, even though both our functions as well as our Apéry limits are a priori algebraic, we continue to get striking conclusions when we apply the Diophantine extensions in section 2 of the holonomy bounds to the case of the system {1,H,H2,…,Hk}\{1,H,H^{2},\ldots,H^{k}\}, for an optimal choice of the power k<rk<r. We can write down explicit entire holomorphic maps φ\varphi that apply to every local system of ramification type (2,2,∙)(2,2,\bullet) on 𝐏1∖{α,β,∞}\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{\alpha,\beta,\infty\}, as follows:

Let α≠β\alpha\neq\beta, and let f∈𝐂​⟦x⟧f\in\mathbf{C}\llbracket x\rrbracket be a holomorphic function germ which analytically continues as a meromorphic function along all paths in 𝐏1∖{α,β,∞}\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{\alpha,\beta,\infty\}, with monodromy of order 22 around both α\alpha and β\beta.

    ψα,β∗​f\psi_{\alpha,\beta}^{*}f is meromorphic on 𝐂\mathbf{C}, where ψα,β​(z)=α+β2⋅(1−cosh⁡(zα​β))+α​β⋅sinh⁡(zα​β)=z+…\displaystyle{\psi_{\alpha,\beta}(z)=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\cdot\left(1-\cosh\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{\alpha\beta}}\right)\right)+\sqrt{\alpha\beta}\cdot\sinh\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{\alpha\beta}}\right)}=z+\ldots.

    Suppose moreover that ff extends analytically at z=αz=\alpha along some path γ\gamma from 00 to α\alpha. The entire holomorphic maps ψα,β\psi_{\alpha,\beta} and φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta} have growth orders 11 and 1/21/2, respectively.

If |α|<|β||\alpha|<|\beta|, and the path γ\gamma lies within the disc of radius |α||\alpha|, then one can take u=tanh−1⁡(α/β)u=\tanh^{-1}(\sqrt{\alpha/\beta}) to be given by the corresponding convergent power series. Lemma 3.2 can be verified by an elementary but unenlightening calculation, so instead we give some hints as to where these formulas come from. For the first claim, we can pull back via a quadratic map ramifying over α\alpha and β\beta, and thus reduce to the case 𝐏1∖{1,∞}\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{1,\infty\} with monodromy 𝐙\mathbf{Z} and universal covering map ψ~​(z)=1−e−z\widetilde{\psi}(z)=1-e^{-z}. One can now successively iterate these quadratic maps, and the limit converges—in some neighborhood of z=0z=0—to φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta} (where the choice of γ\gamma determines uu).

3.2 An effective irrationality type for high order roots.

Whereas the x=−1/nx=-1/n specialization to 1−xr\sqrt[r]{1-x} in Eq. 3.1 directly constructs a sequence of rational approximations to 1+1/nr\sqrt[r]{1+1/n} which converge fast enough to supply an effective irrationality measure μ→2\mu\to 2 in the limit n≫r1n\gg_{r}1, historically it was not easy to obtain any nontrivial effective irrationality measure for 2r\sqrt[r]{2} for large rr. This had to wait until 1971 with the first of Baker’s Sharpening series of papers [5]. The asymptotic bound μeff​(2r)≪log⁡r\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}(\sqrt[r]{2})\ll\log{r} in [6] is, up to the absolute constant, still the state-of-art today. But Theorem 2.6 with the dihedral algebraic construction work together to directly supply a sub-Liouville effective bound μeff​(2r)≪r​(log⁡r)3\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}(\sqrt[r]{2})\ll\sqrt{r(\log{r})^{3}}. This irrationality measure is essentially of Siegel’s strength, but it is effective, and applies just as well to any binomial algebraic number a/br\sqrt[r]{a/b}. In a way, our argument effectivizes Mahler’s explicit Hermite–Padé treatment [53] of Siegel’s [56] ineffective exponent 2​r2\sqrt{r} for the particular case of binomial numbers a/br\sqrt[r]{a/b} with 0<a<b0<a<b. Thue, Siegel, and Mahler worked with the explicit type I Hermite–Padé form directly for the extended binomial system {1,(1−x)1/r,…,(1−x)k/r}\{1,(1-x)^{1/r},\ldots,(1-x)^{k/r}\} and, with an optimal choice of k<rk<r, specialized x:=1−a​q0r/b​p0r≈0x:=1-aq_{0}^{r}/bp_{0}^{r}\approx 0 for a hypothetical exceptionally good “anchoring” approximation p0/q0≈a/brp_{0}/q_{0}\approx\sqrt[r]{a/b}. By Baker’s theorem, such a “Thue ghost lever” p0/q0p_{0}/q_{0} is known to not exist, and this is the ultimate source of the ineffectivity in the whole Thue paradigm. In contrast, we work with the “dual” system {1,H,…,Hk}\{1,H,\ldots,H^{k}\} where HH is the dihedral algebraic generating function of the Hermite–Padé forms of {1,(1−x)1/r}\{1,(1-x)^{1/r}\}, specialized directly at the requisite point x=1−a/b∈(0,1)∩𝐐x=1-a/b\in(0,1)\cap\mathbf{Q}. The growth properties of the entire multivalent maps of Lemma 3.2 (2) are restricted to a suitable choice of radius, and input into Proposition 2.4. The ensuing holonomy bound enables us to make a choice of k=m−1k=m-1 closely similar to Siegel’s (and, by extension, Mahler’s) optimizing choice, but now the Diophantine bound is effective as we have used the multivalence of φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}, in place of the ghost Thue lever p0/q0p_{0}/q_{0}, for increasing the overconvergence as far as possible.

Concretely in our 2r\sqrt[r]{2} example, consider H⁡(y):=B1/r​(−1,y)−21/r​A1/r​(−1,y)∈𝐐⁡⟦y⟧+21/r​𝐐​⟦y⟧H(y):=B_{1/r}(-1,y)-2^{1/r}A_{1/r}(-1,y)\in\mathbf{Q}\llbracket y\rrbracket+2^{1/r}\mathbf{Q}\llbracket y\rrbracket from Proposition 3.1, where the corresponding ODE has singularities at α=3−2​2\alpha=3-2\sqrt{2} (the overconvergent singularity) and β=3+2​2\beta=3+2\sqrt{2}. With K=𝐐K=\mathbf{Q}, we have 𝐛=𝟎\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}, and the pp-adic convergence radii have Rp=1R_{p}=1, for p∤rp\nmid r, and ∏p|rRp−1=r​∏p|rp1/(p−1)\prod_{p\mid r}R_{p}^{-1}=r\prod_{p\mid r}p^{1/(p-1)}. 3.3 A new proof of the transcendence of π\pi and other logarithms.

If we take the ν→0\nu\to 0 limit of Eq. 3.3, we obtain an ODE whose solutions are given by A(x,y):=(1−4y+2xy+x2y2)−1/2A(x,y):=\left(1-4y+2xy+x^{2}y^{2}\right)^{-1/2} and B⁡(x,y):=2​A​(x,y)​log⁡(1−x⁡(1+x​y−1−4​y+2​x​y+x2​y2)/2)B(x,y):=2A(x,y)\log{\left(1-x\left(1+xy-\sqrt{1-4y+2xy+x^{2}y^{2}}\right)/2\right)}, and such that H:=B⁡(x,y)−log⁡(1−x)​A​(x,y)H:=B(x,y)-\log(1-x)A(x,y) is the yy-generating series of the diagonal Hermite–Padé approximants of the logarithm function [34, § 3.3.7]. The domain y∈𝐏1∖{((1±1−x)/x),∞}y\in\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{((1\pm\sqrt{1-x})/x),\infty\} and overconvergence property of HH are exactly the same as in the discussion with the algebraic dihedral functions in subsection 3.1, but now HH is a transcendental function with an infinite dihedral monodromy D∞≅(𝐙/2​𝐙)∗(𝐙/2​𝐙)D_{\infty}\cong(\mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z})\ast(\mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z}), and correspondingly B∈𝐐⁡[x]​⟦y⟧B\in\mathbf{Q}[x]\llbracket y\rrbracket has [1,…,n][1,\ldots,n] type denominators. Examining the analog of the holonomy quotients Eq. 3.9 and Eq. 3.12 leads in this context to a new proof of the transcendence of the complex and pp-adic logarithms log⁡a\log{a} at all algebraic arguments a=1−x∈𝐐¯×∖{1}↪𝐂a=1-x\in\overline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\times}\smallsetminus\{1\}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{C} or a∈𝐐¯×∖μp∞↪𝐂pa\in\overline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\times}\smallsetminus\mu_{p^{\infty}}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{C}_{p} with |1−a|p<1|1-a|_{p}<1. We illustrate this on the case of π\pi (with x=2x=2). Replacing yy by i​ziz, we apply the dihedral method to H⁡(z):=B⁡(z)−π​A​(z)H(z):=B(z)-\pi A(z) on z∈𝐏1∖{−1/2,1/2,∞}z\in\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{-1/2,1/2,\infty\}, where:

(3.13) A(z):=(1−4z2)−1/2∈𝐙⟦z⟧,B(z):=−2A(z)arcsin(2z)∈∑n≥0zn​𝐙[1,…,n].A(z):=(1-4z^{2})^{-1/2}\in\mathbf{Z}\llbracket z\rrbracket,\quad B(z):=-2A(z)\arcsin(2z)\in\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{z^{n}\,\mathbf{Z}}{[1,\ldots,n]}.

At this point, taking again the maps φ−1/2,1/2(R2z)\varphi_{-1/2,1/2}(R^{2}z) at one (the “overconvergent”) embedding K↪𝐂K\hookrightarrow\mathbf{C} and ψ−1/2,1/2(Rz)\psi_{-1/2,1/2}(Rz) at the d−1d-1 other complex embeddings, the—qualitative, for simplicity—holonomy quotient bound similar to Eq. 3.9 becomes k+1≪R/(d+1d​log⁡R−∑j=1k1/j),k+1\ll R\big/\left(\frac{d+1}{d}\log{R}-\sum_{j=1}^{k}1/j\right), provided a positive denominator. In contrast, the x=2x=2 specialization considered above does not even directly give a sequence of rational numbers converging to π\pi, but yet still leads to the transcendence of π\pi, and even to explicit (if not impressive) irrationality measures such as μ⁡(π)≤15.086\mu(\pi)\leq 15.086.

4 Conclusion of the new proof of Theorem 1.1.

In Propositions 3.3 and 3.4 we constructed a monotonic function g=gK,v:𝐑≥0→𝐑>1g=g_{K,v}:\mathbf{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbf{R}_{>1} which can be made fully explicit, depending only on KK and vv and having limx→∞g⁡(x)=∞\lim_{x\to\infty}g(x)=\infty, such that, for all r∈𝐍r\in\mathbf{N} possessing a factor l≍1+h⁡(a)l\asymp 1+h(a), resp. a factor l≍r⁡(1+h⁡(a))l\asymp\sqrt{r(1+h(a))} congruent to 1modp1\mod{p}, the following lower bound in two logarithms holds uniformly for all places u|vu\mid v of K⁡(ar)K(\sqrt[r]{a}) and all elements a,η∈Ka,\eta\in K:

The next type of argument to conclude Theorem 1.1 is due to Bombieri [17, § 8] and is now standard. The simplest form of [17, Lemma 4] is:

Lemma 4.1.

Consider n1,…,nt∈𝐙n_{1},\ldots,n_{t}\in\mathbf{Z} and two integer parameters Q,N∈𝐍Q,N\in\mathbf{N}. There exists a positive integer rr of the form r=Q!​N/qr=Q!N/q for some q∈{1,…,Q}q\in\{1,\ldots,Q\} and rational integers p1,…,pt∈𝐙p_{1},\ldots,p_{t}\in\mathbf{Z} satisfying

Dirichlet’s approximation theorem applied to the vector (n1/Q!​N,…,nt/Q!​N)(n_{1}/Q!N,\ldots,n_{t}/Q!N) and with QQ as the Dirichlet parameter gives a simultaneous rational approximation (p1/q,…,pt/q)(p_{1}/q,\ldots,p_{t}/q) with some common denominator q∈{1,…,Q}q\in\{1,\ldots,Q\} for which Eq. 4.3 holds with r:=Q!​N/q∈𝐍r:=Q!N/q\in\mathbf{N}.

5 Irrationality measures: Examples.

We finish with two illustrative examples of Theorem 2.6 and its variants. The first is an irrationality measure for L⁡(2,χ−3)L(2,\chi_{-3}), making one of the main irrationality results of [34] effective (see Remark 2.7). The second is the irrationality of ζ2​(5)∈𝐐2\zeta_{2}(5)\in\mathbf{Q}_{2}, which in early 2020 had been our first joint result in this collaboration.

5.2 The irrationality of ζ2​(5)∈𝐐2\zeta_{2}(5)\in\mathbf{Q}_{2}.

Let 𝒲+\mathcal{W}^{+} be the space of continuous homomorphisms κ:𝐙p×→𝐂p×\kappa:\mathbf{Z}^{\times}_{p}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}^{\times}_{p} with κ⁡(−1)=1\kappa(-1)=1. The pp-adic zeta function ζp​(κ)\zeta_{p}(\kappa) is a rigid analytic function on 𝒲+\mathcal{W}^{+} away from the point κ=1\kappa=1, at which it has a simple pole. If κ\kappa has the form x↦χ⁡(x)​xkx\mapsto\chi(x)x^{k} for an integer kk, then ζp​(κ)=Lp​(χ,1−k)\zeta_{p}(\kappa)=L_{p}(\chi,1-k), where Lp​(χ,k)L_{p}(\chi,k) is the Kubota–Leopoldt pp-adic LL-function [47]. If κ\kappa has the form x↦x2​kx\mapsto x^{2k} for an integer kk, then we write ζp​(1+2​k):=ζp​(κ)\zeta_{p}(1+2k):=\zeta_{p}(\kappa). For complex ss, write ζ∗​(s)=(1−p−s)​ζ​(s)\zeta^{*}(s)=(1-p^{-s})\zeta(s) for the pp-deprived zeta function, that is, the usual Riemann zeta function with the local factor at pp removed. For a negative integer kk, there is an equality

(5.2) ζp​(1+2​k)=ζ∗​(1+2​k)\zeta_{p}(1+2k)=\zeta^{*}(1+2k)

which should be interpreted as meaning that both values (a priori elements of 𝐂p\mathbf{C}_{p} and 𝐂\mathbf{C} respectively) are both inside 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and are equal. For a positive integer kk, the continuity of ζp​(κ)\zeta_{p}(\kappa) together with Eq. 5.2 implies the equality

(5.3) ζp​(1+2​k)=limm→kζ∗​(1+2​m),\zeta_{p}(1+2k)=\lim_{m\rightarrow k}\zeta^{*}(1+2m),

where the limit is is over m∈𝐙m\in\mathbf{Z} subject to the condition that 2​m≡2​kmodp−12m\equiv 2k\bmod p-1 and the topology on 𝐙\mathbf{Z} is induced from the inclusion 𝐙⊂𝐙p\mathbf{Z}\subset\mathbf{Z}_{p}. One can view Eq. 5.3 as interpolating the Kummer congruences on the Bernoulli numbers. The characterization of ζp​(1+2​k)\zeta_{p}(1+2k) relevant for us is that, for any 2​k∈𝐙∖{0}2k\in\mathbf{Z}\smallsetminus\{0\}, it is the unique pp-adic number for which the formal power series

As far as the qualitative irrationality in Theorem 5.2 is concerned, the proof of ζ2​(5)∉𝐐\zeta_{2}(5)\notin\mathbf{Q} neither requires the full force of the holonomy bounds in [34], nor even of their precursors in [35]. Indeed, the proof goes through (with the same φ∞\varphi_{\infty} corresponding to Ωcirc\Omega^{\mathrm{circ}}) even after replacing the Bost–Charles integral term in the numerator by sup𝐓log⁡|φ|\sup_{\mathbf{T}}\log|\varphi|, and τ⁡(𝐛)\tau(\mathbf{b}) by τ=5\tau=5. The corresponding computation for Eq. 5.6 is:

(5.8) 6≤m≤max⁡log⁡|φ⁡(z)|+∑plog⁡Rplog⁡|φ′​(0)|+∑plog⁡Rp−τ=log⁡((1/5)​∏n=1∞(1+(1/5)n)24)+12​log⁡2−log⁡3+12​log⁡2−5=5.52667​…<6.6\leq m\leq\frac{\max\log|\varphi(z)|+\sum_{p}\log R_{p}}{\log|\varphi^{\prime}(0)|+\sum_{p}\log R_{p}-\tau}=\frac{\log\left((1/5)\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1+(1/5)^{n})^{24}\right)+12\log 2}{-\log 3+12\log 2-5}=5.52667\ldots<6.

We proved such bounds (together with the application to ζ2​(5)\zeta_{2}(5)) in 2020 (see [34, §15.7]), but we put the argument aside in order to work towards the main theorems of [34]; we apologize for the delay! Quite recently, Lai, Sprang, and Zudilin [50] have found a completely new proof of the irrationality of ζ2​(5)\zeta_{2}(5), more in the spirit of Apéry’s original argument, by working with a differential equation with better convergence properties. The corresponding local system in their case appears to have a genuinely different geometric origin, coming from a moduli space of Calabi–Yau 33-folds rather than a symmetric power of the Picard–Fuchs equation of a modular curve. Neither of these results, however, have any direct bearing on the (ir)rationality of the classical ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5).22 2 One may wonder why one can prove the irrationality of ζ2​(5)∈𝐐2\zeta_{2}(5)\in\mathbf{Q}_{2} but not the irrationality of ζ⁡(5)∈𝐑\zeta(5)\in\mathbf{R}. We give a heuristic explanation why the first problem is easier. Let ℳ​𝒯​(𝐙)\mathcal{MT}(\mathbf{Z}) denote the Tannakian category of mixed Tate motives over 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. Associated to ℳ​𝒯​(𝐙)\mathcal{MT}(\mathbf{Z}) is a 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-algebra of real (fixed by complex conjugation) motivic periods 𝒫\mathcal{P} [27]. The comparison theorem between Betti cohomology and de Rham cohomology (over 𝐂\mathbf{C}) induces a period map 𝒫→𝐑\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathbf{R}, and Grothendieck’s period conjecture implies that this map is injective [3]. A consequence of this conjecture is that the 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-algebra generated by ζ⁡(2)\zeta(2) and the odd values ζ⁡(2​k+1)\zeta(2k+1) for k≥1k\geq 1 is free on these generators; equivalently, that these values are all transcendental and moreover algebraically independent. What is perhaps surprising at first is that the pp-adic analogue of this story behaves somewhat differently [14, 45]. One of the most basic manifestations of this difference is that the pp-adic comparison theorem naturally places the pp-adic analogue of 2​π​i2\pi i as an element in BdR+B^{+}_{\mathrm{dR}} which maps to zero in 𝐂p\mathbf{C}_{p}. In particular, the only sensible definition of ζp​(2)\zeta_{p}(2) returns ζp​(2)=0\zeta_{p}(2)=0 ([63, Rem 3.7]). One nonetheless conjectures [64] that the 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-algebra 𝐐⁡(ζp​(3),ζp​(5),ζp​(7),…)\mathbf{Q}(\zeta_{p}(3),\zeta_{p}(5),\zeta_{p}(7),\ldots) is free (on the obvious generators). Let us consider how the vanishing of ζp​(2)\zeta_{p}(2) affects approaches to irrationality. The first step in any Apéry type scheme is to produce a motivic local system where the corresponding LL-value arises as a period. One issue, when trying to construct such local systems is that various periods get “mixed” together and it is hard to separate the period one is particularly interested in. (One interesting discussion of these issues from a geometric point of view can be found in [28].) The point is now that, pp-adically, the vanishing of ζp​(2)\zeta_{p}(2) makes it easier to realize the odd zeta values on their own. Relevantly for us, the construction in [33] directly generalizes to produce an ODE over 𝐏1∖{0,−1/26,∞}\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,-1/2^{6},\infty\} associated to ζ2​(2​k+1)\zeta_{2}(2k+1) for any kk; we know of no simple analogous construction for ζ⁡(2​k+1)∈𝐑\zeta(2k+1)\in\mathbf{R}. As another example; the ODE for the 22-adic Catalan’s constant in [33] has the form ℒ​F=0\mathcal{L}F=0 over 𝐏1∖{0,−1/24,∞}\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,-1/2^{4},\infty\} where ℒ=x​(1+16​x)2​d2d​x2+(1+16​x)2​dd​x−4.\mathcal{L}=x(1+16x)^{2}\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}}+(1+16x)^{2}\frac{d}{dx}-4. Up to scaling this is a hypergeometric equation which one can solve explicitly, namely, with: (5.9) A⁡(x)=(1+16​x)1/2⋅F12​[.1/2​1/21.;−16​x],C⁡(x)=(1+16​x)1/2⋅F12​[.1/2​1/21.;1+16​x].A(x)=(1+16x)^{1/2}\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{1/2,1/2}{1};-16x\right]},\qquad C(x)=(1+16x)^{1/2}\cdot{}_{2}F_{1}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{1/2,1/2}{1};1+16x\right]}. The holomorphic solution B⁡(x)∈𝐐​⟦x⟧B(x)\in\mathbf{Q}\llbracket x\rrbracket to the non-homogenous equation ℒ​F=1+16​x\mathcal{L}F=1+16x with B⁡(0)=0B(0)=0 and B′​(0)=1B^{\prime}(0)=1 is of denominator type τ=[1,2,…,n]2\tau=[1,2,\ldots,n]^{2}. Another solution to this equation ℒ​F=1+16​x\mathcal{L}F=1+16x is given explicitly by D(x)=−1+16​x4⋅F23[.1​1​13/2​3/2.;1+16x].D(x)=-\frac{1+16x}{4}\cdot{}_{3}F_{2}{\left[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{1,1,1}{3/2,3/2};1+16x\right]}. Over the real numbers, D⁡(x)D(x) is singular at x=0x=0, and we have the equality (5.10) D⁡(x)=B⁡(x)−G2⋅A⁡(x)−π216⋅C⁡(x),D(x)=B(x)-\frac{G}{2}\cdot A(x)-\frac{\pi^{2}}{16}\cdot C(x), where G∈𝐑G\in\mathbf{R} is now the usual Catalan’s constant. In contrast, 22-adically, we see that D⁡(x)D(x) converges for |1+16​x|2<24|1+16x|_{2}<2^{4}, or for |x|2<28|x|_{2}<2^{8}, and so it is certainly regular at x=0x=0. Now the 22-adic avatar of Eq. 5.10 simplifies to the formula (5.11) D⁡(x)=B⁡(x)−G22⋅A⁡(x),D(x)=B(x)-\frac{G_{2}}{2}\cdot A(x), in which G2∈𝐐2G_{2}\in\mathbf{Q}_{2} is the 22-adic Catalan constant. Thus Eq. 5.11 realizes G2G_{2} as an Apéry limit. The key point is now that Eq. 5.10 is precisely the “same” equation as Eq. 5.11 as long as we interpret the 22-adic meaning of (2​π​i)2(2\pi i)^{2} to be zero, but Apéry’s method only allows one to deduce that G2∈𝐐2∖𝐐G_{2}\in\mathbf{Q}_{2}\smallsetminus\mathbf{Q}, but not that G∈𝐑∖𝐐G\in\mathbf{R}\smallsetminus\mathbf{Q}. That said, while this is an argument to explain why the pp-adic zeta values of small weight should be easier to study than their Archimedean counterparts, there is also the contrasting remark that we can’t as yet even rule out the possibility that ζp​(3)=0\zeta_{p}(3)=0 for all sufficiently large pp, let alone prove that all those values are irrational.
